style: Narrate as a warm, confident, human product-film narrator. Natural and engaging, at a brisk but unhurried pace: short breaths between sentences, light emphasis on key words, genuine enthusiasm without hype. Never robotic or sing-song.

scenes.vo: Jezero Crater: an ancient lake bed on Mars, where NASA's Perseverance rover is searching for signs of past life. Now imagine planning your own walk there.

We're Binary Explorers. Imam Hosen, our team lead, architected and built the system. Ahad, our NASA data analyst, verified every dataset. And Biswadev, our 3D designer and QA tester, shaped the visuals and tested every feature.
We love Mars, and we kept hitting the same wall: the data is public, but the tools rarely show where an answer came from. So we built one that always does.
NASA publishes thirteen hundred Mars datasets, elevation down to one metre, and the rover's path sol by sol. All open... but scattered.

Who feels that? A student asking why Jezero was chosen. A teacher who wants a real mission in class. One day, the first crews to walk on Mars. And when a chatbot invents a coordinate, no one can check it.
Signals take up to twenty-two minutes between Earth and Mars, so crews must plan on their own. The opportunity: NASA's evidence, and its limits, in one place you can trace.
Our big idea: a Martian map built only on NASA evidence. Switch Trek layers, scrub Perseverance sol by sol, and add official feature names and HiRISE terrain models from data dot NASA dot gov.
The Left on Mars layer shows every lander and rover NASA has operated on Mars. Drag the timeline from 1976 to today, and watch each one fall silent.

Draw a Marswalk, or load Perseverance's real route. The terrain is sampled from NASA's elevation model, every Risk Index component cites its source, and the cockpit names the craters and terrain models along the way.
Pick two points for a slope-aware A-star corridor, always non-certifying, then fly it in 3D over HiRISE imagery.
Presets, Classroom Mode, a command palette, focus mode and share links are one click away, and briefings export to Markdown or PDF.
The mission agent picks its tools, runs them in parallel, and streams an answer. Every number it states is checked against a tool result, and the provenance drawer shows where each one came from.
Ask the corpus, and every sentence carries a citation, in English or in Bangla. Retrieval previews live, and new documents are indexed in seconds.
Pull the wifi, and it still works: every source falls back to a verified cache, and Open Data still searches every Mars dataset.
Earth gets its own lane: live EONET wildfires and storms on NASA's own satellite imagery, never mixed into a Mars decision.
Every page tells a 3D data story: Earth and Mars at true scale, Jezero cell by cell, the traverse by sol, every NASA landing, slopes in relief, and a route raised into an elevation curtain.
Every page adds to the story: Earth widgets, the source register, targets, a guided tour, run traces, the architecture, a gallery, model comparisons, Earth analogs and a mission card.
It's open source under Apache 2.0, with all AI use disclosed, built for challenge eleven. Next, we need science mentors and classroom pilots.
One day, the first crew could rehearse their Marswalk right here, with NASA's evidence at every step. Mars Explorer... from Binary Explorers.
